summary: Learners aged 7–11 learn to draw and read the canonical particle (dot) diagrams for solids (particles close, in a regular pattern, vibrating in place), liquids (close, irregularly arranged, sliding past each other), and gases (far apart, moving fast in random directions). The diagram is a reasoning tool: from it learners explain fixed shape, flow, and compressibility. Two conventions must be taught precisely — (1) the particles themselves do not change size, colour, number or state across states; only spacing, pattern and motion change; and (2) the space between gas particles is empty, not filled with air. Teach a static arrangement snapshot first, then add motion. Learners sketch before/after a state change (e.g. melting) and annotate what changed, linking to heating and cooling.
misconceptions: Particles themselves expand, melt, change colour or change state (attributing macroscopic properties to particles).
The space between particles is filled with air/gas rather than being empty.
Gas particles sit only at the bottom of a container.
Particle size or number changes between states, rather than only spacing and motion.
Solids' particles are completely still (they actually vibrate in place).

activities.title: Particle diagram lab: place, play, and test
steps: Choose a state and place particles accordingly: a solid in neat regular rows, a liquid close together but disordered, a gas spread far apart.

Add motion to the arrangement — show solid particles vibrating in place without leaving their spots, liquid particles sliding and tumbling over each other, and gas particles scattering and bouncing off the walls.

Run a 'squash the container' test and observe compression qualitatively: the gas visibly compresses as its empty gaps get smaller, while the solid and liquid show very little change (they are hard to compress, not perfectly incompressible).
Watch a running count of particles stay the same across every state, and keep every dot the same size when switching states, to show number and size are conserved.

Model melting: take the solid and show its particles loosening out of the regular pattern into a disordered arrangement and speeding up — staying close together (still touching, not moving far apart; only a small spacing change) and remaining the same particles — then annotate what changed.
activities.insight: A particle diagram becomes a working model only when it both shows arrangement and moves: from it a learner can explain why solids keep shape, liquids flow, and gases can be squashed, and why heating to melt rearranges and speeds up particles without changing the particles themselves.

activities.title: Canonical reference and hand-drawing on paper
steps: Study a reference of the three canonical diagrams, each labelled with its arrangement, spacing and motion.
For each diagram, read the accompanying 'what this explains' note (fixed shape, flow, or compressibility) and connect the picture to the property.
Draw all three diagrams by hand on paper, keeping dots the same size and leaving gas gaps empty, then label arrangement and motion for each.
activities.insight: Fluent recall and hand-production of the canonical conventions anchors the representation so it can be used without a prompt; a reference supports memory but the learner must still produce the diagrams independently.

activities.title: Read it and draw it: two-way check
steps: Point to which of two given diagrams (dots spread far apart vs dots packed in a regular grid) is the gas and which is the solid, and explain the decision by spacing and arrangement.
On a blank box, draw the particles for a liquid — close together and touching but irregularly arranged — and add marks showing them sliding and flowing past each other.

Answer probing questions: In your liquid drawing, are the particles touching or apart, and how does that explain why water is very hard to squash? What's in the space between gas particles, and how do you know? When your solid melts, which parts of the picture change and which stay the same — do the dots themselves (their size and number) change, or is it the arrangement and motion that change while spacing changes only a little?
Critique a flawed example — 'someone drew big dots for gas and small dots for ice' — and say what you'd tell them.
activities.insight: Translating both ways — reading a given diagram AND generating a new one — catches errors a single direction hides, confirming the representation carries the meaning rather than being memorised.

checkQuestion: Show the child a particle diagram of a gas (a few dots spread far apart in a box) and one of a solid (dots packed in a regular grid). First: 'Point to the gas and the solid — how did you decide?' Then hand them a blank box and say: 'Now YOU draw the particles for a liquid, and add little marks to show how they're moving.' Watch both the reading and the drawing.
checkAnswer: Reads the widely-spaced dots as gas and the packed regular grid as solid, justified by SPACING and ARRANGEMENT. Then draws a liquid as particles still close together (touching) but irregularly arranged, with movement marks showing them sliding/flowing past each other — not a neat grid (solid) and not far apart (gas). Same-size dots throughout; nothing drawn in the gaps.
